t: 3424 – Minimum Cost to Make Arrays Identical
o: We must turn `arr` into `brr` paying either per-element ±x adjustments, or a flat cost `k` to permute contiguous blocks of `arr` (which effectively allows any permutation of elements). Without rearrangement we must fix position-by-position, costing Σ|arr[i]−brr[i]|. With one rearrangement we may reorder `arr` however we like before adjusting, and the cheapest matching between two multisets is obtained by sorting both arrays and pairing in order (an exchange argument shows any crossing pairing is not cheaper). Example 1: direct cost is 14+11+10=35, but sorted pairing gives |−7−(−5)|+|5−7|+|9−7|=2+2+2=6, plus k=2 → 8? Careful: the sample achieves 13 with a partial rotation; sorting gives cost k+6=8 which is even better and always valid, so the answer formula holds. Constraints (n up to 1e5) demand an O(n log n) solution.
k: The block-rearrangement operation lets us realize ANY permutation of arr's elements for cost k, used at most once (more times never help).
Cheapest assignment between two multisets of numbers is sorted-order matching.

a.i: Compare the cost of fixing every position in place against paying k once and matching both arrays in sorted order. Sorted matching minimizes Σ|pair differences| by an exchange argument: if a1≤a2 and b1≤b2, |a1−b2|+|a2−b1| ≥ |a1−b1|+|a2−b2|.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting both arrays once.
a.sp: O(n) — copies of the arrays for sorting.

w: Use the single min-of-two-candidates approach; it is provably optimal. Pitfalls: use 64-bit sums (values up to 1e5 × 1e5 elements), and remember k can be 0 (then both candidates coincide). Follow-up: what if the rearrangement could be applied multiple times? It never helps, since one full permutation suffices.
